content:
As someone who's been mainly self-taught their whole life, I'm one who believes in finding a good hands-on applied project.

I find this has been something that's rather difficult for newcomers since a lot of concepts, doctrines, and principles from formal methods and/or languages (like Lean ITP) tend to be rather theoretical.

Anyone willing to help me brainstorm how to shepherd people towards finding their own learning applications would be greatly appreciated.

As I started learning Lean, the thing that helped me the most was to write specifications for other applications I wanted to build as Lean proofs and then have an LLM translate the proof for that inti a different programming language (maybe several different programming languages even).

While this pattern worked really well for me, a lot of people find it quite befuddling: why would you write an application twice?

I suppose I've learned that my thought patterns are somewhat averse to other people's. so I'm trying to understand what works better for others.

A bit late to answer this i guess, but since you can use Lean for a lot it really depends. I'm still learning myself, and I try to solve some coding problems in Lean as well as follow along with a textbook using Lean.

One answer for me is solving Project Euler problems and verifying the correctness of the source code doing the computations (for all meaningful inputs, not only for the specific one that's given in Project Euler).
(It's in Rocq and C right now for me, but the same can be done in Lean.)

So basically the same answer as for you, I believe, except these problems are tinier than any application. Applications are for later plans, when I get more confident.
